forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

compliance.notes: Strong core compliance: full prudential-indicator suite (Appendix 14) with an exemplary liability benchmark charted to ~2072, authorised-limit/operational-boundary derivation with headroom rationale, an SLY-driven counterparty matrix using CDS beyond ratings (Appendix 3), a PWLB no-yield certification, an annuity/asset-life MRP policy and a genuinely strategic capital investment strategy (Appendix 9). Weakest areas are disclosure/reporting formalities - no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05) or financial-instruments accounting disclosures (RPT-06) in scope, no quantitative portfolio risk-exposure indicator (INV-06), and light treatment of commercial-investment formalities (no explicit PC paras 51-53 compliance statement, exit-options review, aggregate commercial limit, or guarantees/contingent-liability identification).

news_drafts.headline: Southend-on-Sea drew £25.1m from set-aside funds as Children's Services overspent by £11.6m in 2025-26
news_drafts.lead:
Southend-on-Sea City Council moved £25.1m from money set aside for named purposes (earmarked reserves) into its main account in 2025-26, to cover a £12.0m day-to-day overspend. The council's external auditor, the accountancy firm KPMG, reports that this kept the General Fund balance from falling. Usable reserves, the part the council can actually spend, fell from £182.9m to £166.0m.

The largest overspend was in Children's Services, which reported an £11.6m adverse variance against a revised budget of £54.5m, compared with £6.1m the year before. Spending rose from £55.6m to £66.1m, which KPMG attributes mainly to the rising cost and complexity of residential and fostering placements. The council avoided about £4m in further costs through intervention. Adult Social Care overspent by £5.5m against a revised budget of £60.7m, as care package numbers and costs rose faster than assumed. A further £1.26m came from the collapse of a direct payment provider. The council's forecasts at the fourth month of 2026-27 show overspends continuing: £5.58m in Children's Services and £7.1m in Adult Social Care.

The committee's papers also cover an unexpected overspend at Focal Point Gallery, for which no figure is given. Internal audit found it arose "primarily" from differing assumptions between the service and finance staff over the Local Authority contribution, "and not as a result of any inappropriate expenditure". It has provided an action plan to improve budget setting and monitoring.

news_drafts.headline: Southend-on-Sea forecasts overspend on general fund and housing account for 2026/27, seeks further savings
news_drafts.lead:
Southend-on-Sea City Council is forecasting that it will spend more than it budgeted in 2026/27, on both its general fund (the day-to-day running costs of council services) and its housing revenue account (the separate, ring-fenced account for its own housing stock, paid for by rents). The position is set out in the Financial Performance Report for July 2026, the fourth month of the financial year, which went to the full council on 7 October.

The papers in this extract do not give the size of either overspend. The detailed figures are in an appendix to the report, which is not part of the material reviewed here, so no amounts are reported.

The report asks the council to agree a response. It "requests that the Chief Executive and Executive Director (Finance & Resources) explore all further opportunities to improve the financial position by the year-end." The council is therefore asking its most senior officer and its finance director to find further ways to reduce costs or improve income during the remaining months of the financial year. The report does not say what those options might be, or how much they would need to deliver.

findings.headline: High staff turnover in IRO service identified as creating risk of inconsistent practice; enhanced training being introduced
findings.detail: The review identified high staff turnover combined with organisational change as creating risk of inconsistent understanding and practice among IRO staff. The council is introducing regular refresher training to mitigate these risks and maintain compliance and consistency.
findings.matters: High turnover in critical statutory services creates operational costs, service quality risks, and compliance risks
findings.quote: This will mitigate the risks arising from high staff turnover, organisational change and help maintain compliance and consistency in delivery.

findings.headline: Timeliness of IRO escalation responses inadequate; dispute resolution safeguard not functioning effectively
findings.detail: The review found that responses to IRO escalations are not timely, meaning the formal dispute resolution process is not functioning effectively as a safeguard. This is identified as requiring improvement to ensure escalated concerns are addressed promptly.
findings.matters: Ineffective escalation and dispute resolution processes create risk that safeguarding concerns are not adequately addressed, with associated legal and financial exposure
findings.quote: Improving the timeliness of responses to IRO escalations so that the dispute resolution process functions effectively as a safeguard.

findings.headline: Delays in IRO allocation, first care plan completion and statutory review cycles prevent oversight occurring at earliest stage
findings.detail: The audit identified delays in allocating IROs, completing first care plans, and conducting statutory review cycles. These delays prevent independent oversight from occurring at the earliest possible stage in the care planning process and are identified as requiring action.
findings.matters: Delays in statutory safeguarding processes create potential exposure to safeguarding failures and associated legal and financial liability
findings.quote: Addressing delays in IRO allocation, completion of the first care plan and statutory review cycles to ensure that IRO oversight occurs at the earliest stage and that any delays are promptly challenged.

findings.headline: IRO service control environment weaknesses identified in compliance, timeliness and oversight; 11 actions agreed
findings.detail: An audit review of the Independent Reviewing Service for looked-after children found areas requiring improvement to strengthen the control environment. Specific weaknesses were identified in compliance with policies and procedures, timeliness of activities, and oversight of the IRO service. The council has agreed 11 actions to address these gaps.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses in a major statutory service area create financial risk through potential service disruption, legal liability, remedial costs, and indicate broader control environment issues
findings.quote: The review identified areas where improvements would strengthen the control environment in place, particularly around compliance with policies and procedures in areas like the quality assurance process, timeliness of activities and oversight of the IRO service.

findings.paper_title: Final Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 and Statement of Accounts 2025-26 - covering report
findings.headline: The 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement was updated to reflect pausing of the Local Government Reorganisation decision for Greater Essex, with no other substantive changes.
findings.detail: The AGS was approved by Audit & Governance Committee on 20 July 2026 and subsequently updated after external audit review 'to reflect the updated position following the pausing of the Local Government Reorganisation decision for Greater Essex.' No other substantive changes were made. The paper does not explain the implications of the LGR pause for Southend's governance, financing, or future plans.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation is a material governance event affecting long-term structure and financial arrangements. A pause in previously planned reorganisation requires governance updates, but implications for Southend's financial strategy are not set out in this paper.
findings.quote: the final Annual Governance Statement now reflects the updated position following the pausing of the Local Government Reorganisation decision for Greater Essex

daily_post.headline: Transformation programme proceeds without preset savings targets; benefits to be validated through business cases
daily_post.lead: The council is committing £8m without locked-in quantified returns. If anticipated benefits fail to materialise during implementation, there is no funded alternative to offset the investment, creating risk to revenue sustainability planning.
